subject: maths
card: Tables, timetables, pictograms, bar charts, line graphs and the mean: read the data and answer questions.
title: Graphs and data
seo_title: Bar charts, pictograms, tables and line graphs practice for KS2 (statistics)
description: Free KS2 statistics practice: read tables and timetables, pictograms with half symbols, bar charts, line graphs, and find the mean. Pictures, hints and worked answers for ages 9 to 11.
intro: Data is information, like how many children chose each pet. Tables, pictograms, bar charts and line graphs show it so you can compare and answer questions.

units.title: Tables and timetables
units.blurb: Find the right row and column.

learn.p: Find the row and the column you need, and read the number where they meet. This table shows the pets chosen by a class.
A tally counts in groups of five: four lines with a fifth line across them. So 3 groups of five and 2 more lines is 15 + 2 = 17.
Each column is one bus or train, and each row is a stop. To find how long a journey takes, subtract the start time from the end time.

questions.q: How many children chose a cat?
questions.hint: Find the Cat row.
questions.explain: The Cat row says 6, so 6 children chose a cat.

questions.q: How many children are in the class altogether?
questions.hint: Add up all the numbers.
questions.explain: 8 + 6 + 3 + 4 = 21 children.

questions.q: How many more children chose a dog than a fish?
questions.hint: Find the difference: dog minus fish.
questions.explain: 8 − 3 = 5 more children chose a dog.

questions.q: A tally has 4 groups of five and 2 more lines. What number does it show?
questions.hint: Each group is 5. Count in fives, then add the extra lines.
questions.explain: 4 groups of five = 20, and 2 more makes 22.

questions.q: How many minutes does Bus A take to get from School to Station?
questions.hint: Bus A leaves School at 8:10 and reaches Station at 8:45.
questions.explain: From 8:10 to 8:45 is 35 minutes.

questions.q: You need to be at the Station by 9:00. Which bus should you catch?
questions.hint: Look at the Station row. Which bus arrives before 9:00?
questions.explain: Bus A reaches the Station at 8:45, before 9:00. Bus B arrives at 9:15, which is too late.

units.title: Pictograms
units.blurb: Check the key, then count symbols.

learn.p: In a pictogram, one symbol can stand for more than one thing. Here each circle stands for 2 books, so 3 circles mean 6 books.
Half a circle stands for half of the key. If a circle is 2 books, half a circle is 1 book. So 4 and a half circles mean 8 + 1 = 9 books.
To find how many more, work out both numbers first, then subtract.

questions.q: How many books were read on Monday?
questions.hint: Each circle is 2 books.
questions.explain: 3 circles × 2 = 6 books.

questions.q: How many books were read on Tuesday?
questions.hint: 4 whole circles and a half. Half a circle is 1 book.
questions.explain: 4 circles = 8 books, and the half circle = 1 book. 8 + 1 = 9 books.

questions.q: How many more books were read on Thursday than on Wednesday?
questions.hint: Thursday is 5 circles, Wednesday is 2 circles.
questions.explain: Thursday: 5 × 2 = 10 books. Wednesday: 2 × 2 = 4 books. 10 − 4 = 6 more.

questions.q: How many children chose blue?
questions.hint: Look at the key: each circle is 4 children.
questions.explain: 4 circles × 4 = 16 children.

questions.q: How many children chose green?
questions.hint: 1 whole circle and a half. What is half of 4?
questions.explain: 1 circle = 4 children, half a circle = 2 children. 4 + 2 = 6.

questions.q: In this pictogram, what does half a circle stand for?
questions.hint: A whole circle is 4 children.
questions.explain: Half of 4 is 2, so half a circle stands for 2 children.

units.title: Bar charts
units.blurb: Read the top of each bar on the scale.

learn.p: Look across from the top of the bar to the scale on the side. Here the Grape bar reaches 9.
The scale doesn't always go up in 1s. It might go up in 2s, 5s or 10s. Work out what each line is worth before you read the bars.
The tallest bar is the most popular. To find how many more, subtract. To find the total, add all the bars.

questions.q: How many children chose grapes?
questions.hint: Look across from the top of the Grape bar.
questions.explain: The Grape bar reaches 9.

questions.q: How many more children chose apples than pears?
questions.hint: Read both bars, then subtract.
questions.explain: Apple is 7 and Pear is 3. 7 − 3 = 4 more.

questions.q: How many children were asked altogether?
questions.hint: Add all four bars.
questions.explain: 7 + 4 + 9 + 3 = 23 children.

questions.q: How many cars went past the school on Wednesday?
questions.hint: The scale goes up in 5s.
questions.explain: The Wednesday bar reaches the line for 35.

questions.q: How many cars went past on Tuesday and Thursday together?
questions.hint: Read the two bars and add them.
questions.explain: Tuesday 15 + Thursday 20 = 35 cars, the same as Wednesday on its own.

questions.q: Which day had the fewest cars?
questions.hint: Find the shortest bar.
questions.explain: Tuesday's bar is the shortest, at 15 cars.

units.title: Line graphs
units.blurb: See how something changes over time.

learn.p: A line graph shows how something changes, like the temperature during a day. Time goes along the bottom, and the amount goes up the side.
When the line goes up, the amount is increasing. When it goes down, it is decreasing. A steeper line means a faster change.
Find the time along the bottom, go up to the line, then look across to the scale. Check what each line on the scale is worth: here it goes up in 2s.

questions.q: What was the temperature at 11am?
questions.hint: Go up from 11am to the dot, then across to the scale.
questions.explain: The dot above 11am is level with 12, so it was 12 °C.

questions.q: How much did the temperature rise from 9am to 1pm?
questions.hint: Read both temperatures and find the difference.
questions.explain: At 9am it was 8 °C and at 1pm it was 18 °C. 18 − 8 = 10 degrees.

questions.q: When was it warmest?
questions.hint: Find the highest point on the line.
questions.explain: The highest point is at 1pm, at 18 °C. After that the line goes down.

questions.q: How tall was the plant in week 3?
questions.hint: W3 means week 3.
questions.explain: The dot above W3 is level with 5, so the plant was 5 cm tall.

questions.q: How much did the plant grow between week 3 and week 4?
questions.hint: Read week 3 and week 4, then subtract.
questions.explain: Week 3: 5 cm. Week 4: 8 cm. 8 − 5 = 3 cm.

questions.q: Between which two weeks did the plant grow the most?
questions.hint: Look for the steepest part of the line.
questions.explain: It grew 1 cm, then 2 cm, then 3 cm, then 2 cm. The biggest jump, 3 cm, was from week 3 to week 4.

units.title: The mean (average)
units.blurb: Add them up, then share equally.

learn.p: The **mean** is a kind of average. It's what each one would get if everything were shared out equally.
Add up all the numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are. The mean of 4, 6 and 8 is (4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 3 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
The mean is always between the smallest and the biggest number. If you get a mean bigger than all the numbers, something went wrong.

questions.q: What is the mean of 4, 6 and 8?
questions.hint: Add them, then divide by 3.

questions.q: What is the mean of 3, 5, 7 and 9?
questions.hint: Add the four numbers, then divide by 4.

questions.q: Ben scored 10, 12 and 8 points in three games. What was his mean score?
questions.hint: Add the scores, then divide by 3.

questions.q: Four children have 3, 5, 6 and 10 sweets. They share them out equally. How many does each child get?
questions.hint: Sharing equally is the same as finding the mean.

questions.q: The mean of three numbers is 5. What do the three numbers add up to?
questions.hint: Mean = total ÷ 3, so total = mean × 3.
questions.explain: If the mean is 5, the total is 5 × 3 = 15.

questions.q: The mean of 2, 4 and 9 is worked out as 12. How can you tell this is wrong?
options: The mean can't be bigger than the biggest number
You can't find a mean of three numbers
questions.hint: Where should the mean be, compared with the numbers?
questions.explain: The mean must be between the smallest and biggest numbers. The right answer is (2 + 4 + 9) ÷ 3 = 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
